turns.text: Hello Hannah, come in and take a seat. What would you like to talk about today?
I'm not really sure where to start. I think I'm just anxious all the time, and it's got worse since September.
What happened in September?
I was made deputy head at my school. I've taught Year 4 for eleven years and I loved it, and then the head asked me to step up when our deputy left.
That sounds like recognition of your work.
That's what everyone says. But I keep thinking they picked the wrong person, and that sooner or later someone will notice I have no idea what I'm doing.
What does it look like when that thought arrives?
Mostly Sunday evenings. My chest goes tight and I start rehearsing Monday's staff meeting in my head.
What do you rehearse?
Every possible question someone might ask, and what I'd say. Then what they'd think of me if I got it wrong.
And what do you imagine they would think?
That I'm out of my depth. That they gave the job to a nice Year 4 teacher who can't actually lead.
Has anyone said anything that suggests that?
No. That's the strange thing. Nobody has. It's all in my head.
It is still very real to you.
Very. Last week I rewrote the same email to the governors four times.
Four times. What was the email about?
A change to the behaviour policy. It was two paragraphs. I was afraid Mr Hargreaves, the chair of governors, would think I was stupid.
How does he treat you?
He's been nothing but kind. He told me in September he was delighted. That makes it worse somehow, because I feel I'm lying to him.
Lying to him about what?
About being capable. As if I'm pretending.
Pretending to be what?
Somebody who knows what she's doing. Most days I feel like a child wearing her mother's coat.
That's a vivid image. Whose coat is it?
My mum's, I suppose. She was a headteacher for twenty years.
Tell me about that.
She was brilliant. Everyone in the village still stops me to say what a wonderful head she was. She retired six years ago and they've named a library after her.
And you're now in a similar job.
A deputy's job. But yes. I can't help comparing. Everything I do, I think, would she have done it better?
Does she say that?
Never. She's very supportive on the surface. She says I've always worried too much and I should stop being silly.
How does it land when she says that?
It makes me feel I'm making a fuss. So I don't tell her how bad it is.
What does she not know?
That I'm awake at four every morning. I fall asleep fine, then I'm awake at four going through the to-do list.
What's on the list?
Everything. Timetable changes, the Ofsted prep, a parent complaint, a child I'm worried about. It goes round and round.
How long have you been waking like that?
Since about the second week of term. I drink a lot of coffee to get through the day, which I know doesn't help.
How many cups?
Five or six. And then I can't sit still in the afternoons.
What do you notice in your body during those afternoons?
My heart goes fast. My hands are a bit shaky. Last Thursday I had to leave a meeting to splash my face with water.
Did anyone notice?
I don't think so. I said I was fetching a document.
That sounds like a lot of effort to hide it.
It is. I'm exhausted by the end of every day just from pretending.
Who knows how you are feeling?
My partner Ben knows a bit. He says I should just enjoy it.
How do you feel when he says that?
Guilty, and a bit alone. He means well. He's an engineer, he thinks if something's a problem you fix it.
And you can't just fix this.
No. I wish it were that simple.
Do you have friends at school you can talk to?
Not any more, not really. I used to eat lunch in the Year 4 corridor with the others. Now I'm their line manager and it's awkward.
So you've lost some company along with the promotion.
Yes. I hadn't thought of it like that. I miss them. I miss my class too.
What do you miss most?
The children, honestly. The daily bit where a child gets something for the first time. Now my days are spreadsheets.
Did you want the promotion?
I thought I did. I said yes in the room because I couldn't say no to her. The head. Then I went home and cried.
What were the tears about?
Fear, I think. And that I'd never get to go back.
Would you want to go back?
I don't know. That sounds terrible, doesn't it? After everyone's been so supportive.
It sounds like an honest question.
Nobody has asked me that. They just say well done.
When was the last time you felt properly relaxed?
The summer holidays. We went walking in the Lakes, and I didn't think about school once for ten days.
What was different there?
Nobody expected anything of me. I was just walking. Ben carried the sandwiches.
And then?
The week before term I was a wreck again. I couldn't eat on the Sunday.
Is there anything you have already tried that helped, even a little?
I started writing down what went well each evening. Small things. A child laughing, a good email.
How did that go?
It helped for about two weeks and then I stopped, because I felt silly.
Silly in what way?
As if I were bragging to myself in a notebook.
Noticing what went well is not the same as bragging.
Probably not. It just felt that way.
That sounds worth coming back to. Have you thought about whether there is something particular you'd like from our work?
I'd like to do the job without feeling like a fraud.
What would that look like on a Tuesday?
Walking into a meeting and not rehearsing it first. Sending an email once.
And on a Sunday?
Being able to sit on the sofa in the evening without my stomach in knots.
Those are clear goals. How do you feel now, saying them out loud?
Lighter. A bit tearful, actually.
That's all right. Take a moment.
Sorry. I didn't expect that.
There's nothing to apologise for. What's coming up?
That it's the first time I've told anyone how bad it is. Not even Ben knows about the four a.m.
What would it be like to tell him?
Scary. He'd probably be hurt that I didn't say sooner.
Would that be a reason to keep it to yourself?
I suppose not. I might try this week.
What would help you do that?
If I choose a quiet moment. Not on a Sunday evening, then I'm too wound up.
Saturday morning, perhaps?
Yes, over breakfast. He's always in a good mood then.
And one more small thing. Would you try the evening notebook again, just for a week, even one line?
I could. I'll put it by the kettle so I don't forget.
We're nearly out of time. Is there anything you want to add?
Only that I nearly cancelled this morning. I'm glad I didn't.
I am glad too. Same time next week?
Yes, please. Thank you.
